title: Tutankhamun's famous dagger came from a meteorite; A hidden pattern in the blade reveals how ancient Egyptians forged it- Moneycontrol.com
excerpt: King Tutankhamun’s famous iron dagger was made from a meteorite. Now, a hidden crystalline pattern inside its blade has revealed how ancient Egyptian craftsmen worked with metal from space thousands of years ago.
content:
King Tutankhamun’s famous iron dagger was made from a meteorite. Now, a hidden crystalline pattern inside its blade has revealed how ancient Egyptian craftsmen worked with metal from space thousands of years ago.

King Tutankhamun’s famous dagger. (Image credits: Wikimedia Commons)

  • Tutankhamun's dagger was made from meteorite metal.
  • The dagger's pattern reveals ancient forging techniques.
  • Egyptians used meteoritic iron for thousands of years.

Tutankhamun’s famous iron dagger was made from metal that fell from the sky, but the most significant evidence is not only the material itself but the special pattern within it. That pattern allowed the scientists to uncover how the ancient craftsmen processed the extraterrestrial material to make an intricate weapon.

Howard Carter, who examined the mummy of Tutankhamun in 1925, discovered that the linen wrappings contained two daggers: one with an iron blade and the other, gold. The iron dagger was characterized by a finely crafted blade, a gold handle decorated with cloisonné and granulation, a rock-crystal pommel, and a gold sheath. As mentioned by Daniela Comelli et al. in their 2016 study, The meteoritic origin of Tutankhamun’s iron dagger blade, published in Meteoritics & Planetary Science, the dagger was one of the rare surviving Egyptian iron objects from the period.

Tutankhamun reigned during Egypt’s 18th Dynasty in the 14th century BCE, when bronze remained the dominant material for tools and weapons and widespread iron production had not yet emerged. However, the presence of iron objects at that time does not imply that the Egyptians were in the Iron Age. Comelli et al. reported that there were iron objects that appeared intermittently in the eastern Mediterranean region during the Late Bronze Age.

The chemistry revealed an extraterrestrial origin

The decisive evidence came in 2016. The researchers analysed the dagger in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo using portable X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy without taking any sample of the artifact away from its resting place. The results showed that the blade had 10.8 ± 0.3% nickel and 0.58 ± 0.04% cobalt.

This information became crucial in solving the question. Iron meteorites usually have around 5% and 35% nickel in their composition. Meanwhile, ancient iron items made of earthly ores before the 19th century had no more than 4% nickel, according to Comelli et al. Additionally, the nickel-to-cobalt ratio in the blade was similar to that in iron meteorites. The team therefore concluded that the blade’s composition strongly supported a meteoritic origin.

Though, the 2016 study was careful about what the chemistry could and could not establish. The nickel and cobalt levels strongly supported a meteoritic origin, but they could not identify which meteorite it came from. Comelli et al. stated that further microstructural analysis would be necessary to understand the metalworking process alongside the meteorite classification. This unanswered question led to another investigation.

A pattern inside the blade revealed how it was made

In 2022, Takafumi Matsui, Ryota Moriwaki, Eissa Zidan and Tomoko Arai published a study in Meteoritics & Planetary Science. Instead of simply measuring the blade’s overall chemical composition, the researchers performed nondestructive two-dimensional elemental mapping of its surface at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

Researchers discovered discontinuous nickel bands, structured in certain locations with cubic symmetry and a width of roughly 1 millimetre. This was seen as a sign of the Widmanstätten pattern, a unique crystalline pattern that forms inside iron meteorites. Along with a localized intermediate nickel content of roughly 11.8 ± 0.5%, which closely mirrors the bulk composition found in 2016, these mappings allowed the researchers to conclude that the source material for the blade is likely an octahedrite iron meteorite. They also found randomly scattered sulfur-rich dark patches, which were seen as troilite residues, a sulfur-containing mineral found in iron meteorites.

The internal structure provided more information about the process. Since the Widmanstätten pattern was still intact, the researchers concluded that the raw meteorite had not been melted and cast into a mold. Rather, they theorized that the blade was forged while solid by keeping the heat at around 950°C, a temperature well below the melting point of meteoritic iron.

This is important because it distinguishes two completely different processes. While the dagger shows that Egyptians knew how to work with meteoritic iron and create complex items from it, it does not prove that Egyptians had the technology to smelt iron from earth materials. This evidence shows that the Egyptians knew how to work with a special kind of iron-nickel meteoric alloy in the Bronze Age. According to Matsui et al., the dagger serves as an example of already existing technology of working with meteoritic iron.

The dagger was part of a much older Egyptian tradition

Tutankhamun’s dagger was, however, not the first known artifact made of meteoritic iron discovered in Egypt. Earlier instances of this artistry can be traced back some 2,000 years. As reported by Thilo Rehren et al. in their 2013 article in the Journal of Archaeological Science, there were nine small iron beads found in the prehistoric cemetery of Gerzeh located in northern Egypt. These beads dated about 3200 BCE and thus could be regarded as the oldest iron objects known from Egypt. Using non-destructive neutron radiography and tomography methods, the scientists found out that the beads were made of hammered meteoritic iron rolled into tubes.

The material was not treated like ordinary utilitarian metal. The authors of the 2013 study noted that the beads had been incorporated into a necklace alongside exotic materials including lapis lazuli, gold and carnelian. They argued that this combination indicated that meteoritic iron was regarded as a special material comparable in status to precious metals and gemstones.

The famous burial mask of King Tutankhamun on display at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. (Image credits: Wikimedia Commons)

Another 2013 investigation, by Diane Johnson, Joann Tyldesley, Thomas Lowe, Peter Withers and Monica Grady, reached a similar conclusion. Published in Meteoritics & Planetary Science, the study used scanning electron microscopy and micro-X-ray computed tomography to examine a Gerzeh bead. The researchers found remnants of the meteoritic Widmanstätten pattern, distorted by cold working, along with fragments retaining a nickel concentration of roughly 30%. They concluded that the bead was consistent with a cold-worked iron meteorite.

The two lines of evidence create a striking technological timeline. Egyptian craftsmen worked with meteoritic iron in 3200 BCE to make jewelry beads from metal that was harder and more brittle than copper. Almost two thousand years later, craftspeople made a well-designed iron dagger for a pharaoh out of another meteoritic metal.

This changes the way Tutankhamun’s dagger fits into the history of metallurgy. It was not an inexplicable iron weapon appearing centuries too early, nor is it evidence that Egypt had suddenly developed large-scale iron production during the Bronze Age. Instead, it belongs to a much older tradition in which naturally occurring meteoritic iron could be collected and deliberately transformed into unusual and valuable objects.

Thus, the real finding hidden inside Tutankhamun’s dagger is not simply that ancient Egyptians used metal from space. They had been doing that for thousands of years. The key point is that a Bronze Age blade preserved enough of its original chemistry and microscopic structure for modern scientists to reconstruct where its metal came from and something about how its makers worked it.
